reconcile.note: Keil and Delitzsch argue God's aim in commanding Isaac's sacrifice was Abraham's complete surrender, not the boy's actual death, since the trial never proceeded to the killing.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll condemns the very conception of a God who commands a father to slaughter his son as monstrous, incomprehensible cruelty rather than a test of faith.

quotes.text: Nothing can be more monstrous than the conception of a God who demands sacrifice—of a God who would ask of a father that he murder his son—of a father that he would burn his daughter. It is far beyond my comprehension how any man ever could have believed such an infinite, such a cruel absurdity.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Ingersoll's Rejoinder to Judge Jeremiah S. Black) (1881), on Genesis 22:2.

quotes.text: Is not the sacrifice of a child to a phantom as horrible in Palestine as in India? Why should a God demand a sacrifice from man?
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Ingersoll's Rejoinder to Judge Jeremiah S. Black) (1881), on Genesis 22:2 and Deuteronomy 12:31.

sides.snippet: Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.
sides.verseText: He said, \"Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.\"

sides.snippet: for even their sons and their daughters do they burn in the fire to their gods.
sides.verseText: You shall not do so to Yahweh your God: for every abomination to Yahweh, which he hates, have they done to their gods; for even their sons and their daughters do they burn in the fire to their gods.
